_about: PRO rewrite pass 13: era 4 (the 22 written veteran scenes).

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Last Season in the Stands
scenarios.text: {parent} tells you on the phone that this is the last season he'll make the six-hour drive to watch you. His eyes aren't good at night anymore, he says, and the back seat hurts.

choices.label: Meet him at the fence every game
choices.result: At the fence after every home game, all season. He tells you what he saw from the stands, the same way he did when you were twelve, and you listen to every word.

choices.label: Arrange rides so he keeps coming
choices.result: Rides, arranged with a neighbor and a car service, so the drive stops being the problem. He makes every home game and complains about the driver's music every time.

choices.label: Thank him for every drive
choices.result: A long call, thanking him for every drive, from the first peewee game to this one. He waves it off, and his voice goes quiet in the middle.

scenarios.title: {tyler}'s Second Act
scenarios.text: {tyler} is in the broadcast booth now, wearing a headset and a tie, and he's calling your games. The first time he says your name on air, he pauses a little too long.

choices.label: Have dinner the night before
choices.result: Dinner the night before, at the old diner. He tells you exactly what he'll say on air, and none of it is mean, and some of it is kind.

choices.label: Give him a good story
choices.result: A story for the broadcast, told to him on the field during warmups. He tells it better than you ever could, and it becomes the clip of the week.

choices.label: Laugh about it
choices.result: Every time the camera finds you, you know he's grinning in the booth. You laugh about it with {holder}, and it makes the games lighter.

scenarios.title: The Reunion
scenarios.text: Your high school reunion is the weekend after the season ends. Twenty years, a gym with streamers, and everyone wants to know what the league is really like.

choices.label: Tell stories all night
choices.result: Stories, all night, to a growing circle by the bleachers. Your old friends laugh in the same places they always did, and {best_friend} finishes your sentences.

choices.label: Ask about their lives instead
choices.result: Their lives, asked about, one by one. They're more interesting than the league: a nurse, a farmer, a pilot, a teacher who still remembers your essay.

choices.label: Skip the reunion
choices.result: Skipped, and you see the pictures later online. Everyone looks older, and so do you, and you feel the miss more than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Younger Kicker in Camp
scenarios.text: At thirty-five, you walk into the meeting room and a fourth-round rookie is sitting in your seat. He doesn't know it's your seat. Everyone else does.

choices.label: Take your seat back every day
choices.result: First into the meeting room, every day after that. The seat is yours until it isn't, and you're not going to give it away for free.

choices.label: Teach him
choices.result: Your routine, your wind charts, your nerves: you teach him all of it. It's the right thing, and it makes the room trust you even more.

choices.label: Ask where you stand
choices.result: {coach}, asked plainly in the hallway. It's an open competition, the coach says, and you appreciate the honesty more than the answer.

scenarios.title: The Veteran Minimum
scenarios.text: You're on the veteran minimum, a third of what you made five years ago. The rookie at the next locker drives your old car; he bought it from the dealer you sold it to.

choices.label: Laugh about it with him
choices.result: Laughing about it together, at the lockers. He offers to sell it back to you at a discount, and you decline, and it becomes your running joke.

choices.label: Adjust the budget
choices.result: A smaller budget, built at the kitchen table, and nobody in the house misses the things you cut. You're surprised how little you needed.

choices.label: Kick for the next deal
choices.result: Every practice, like the next deal depends on it, because it does. It's motivating, and on bad days it's heavy.

scenarios.title: The Body Says No
scenarios.text: Your hip takes an hour to warm up now, and Monday mornings take two. The trainer has started calling your warmup 'the ceremony', and the rookies watch it like it's a show.

choices.label: Build a new morning routine
choices.result: A new routine, built from scratch: heat, bands, a long walk, a slow stretch. It takes ninety minutes every morning, and it works.

choices.label: Push through it
choices.result: Through it, every morning, gritting your teeth. Your hip complains all season and holds, and you're tired in a new way.

choices.label: Rest more, practice less
choices.result: Less practice, more rest. You're fresher on game days and stiffer at practice, and you can't decide if it's wisdom or surrender.

scenarios.title: The General Manager's Office
scenarios.text: The general manager calls you into his office and closes the door. They're going in a different direction at kicker next season, he says, and he wanted you to hear it from him.

choices.label: Prove them wrong
choices.result: Here or somewhere else, you'll prove them wrong. The fire is back, and you kick the rest of the season like an audition.

choices.label: Have your agent look around
choices.result: Your agent, looking around quietly. There's interest, modest and real, and two clubs ask to see you in the spring.

choices.label: Tell your family that night
choices.result: Your family, told that night at dinner. Nobody panics, and {parent} tells you he's proud no matter what, which you needed.

scenarios.title: The Broadcast Booth
scenarios.text: A network offers you a job in the broadcast booth when you're done: a three-year deal, a headset, and the chance to explain kicking to millions of people who never understood it.

choices.label: Say yes for later
choices.result: Yes, for later, with a handshake and a contract in a drawer. It's nice to know there's a door on the other side of all this.

choices.label: Ask {tyler}
choices.result: {tyler}, who's been in the booth for two years, tells you everything: the early mornings, the producers, the joy of it. You sign the next week.

choices.label: Keep the door open
choices.result: Not yet, you tell them, warmly. They say they'll ask again, and you believe them, and you put the idea away for later.

scenarios.title: The Coaching Offer
scenarios.text: A college asks if you'd coach their kickers when you retire: a small program, a good school, a field with a view of the mountains, and a head coach who used to be your holder.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.result: Yes, for when the time comes. You start keeping notes on how you teach, and the head coach sends you a photo of your future office.

choices.label: Ask for time to think
choices.result: Time to think, and they give it to you gladly. You visit the campus in the spring and stand on the field for a long time.

choices.label: Stay home after football
choices.result: No, kindly. You want to be home when you're done, every night, for a long time. The college understands and keeps the door open.

choices.label: Tell them what you've learned teaching
choices.result: What you learned teaching younger kickers, explained over lunch. They offer you the job on the spot, and you shake on it.

scenarios.title: The Ring of Honor
scenarios.text: The club wants to put your name in the stadium's ring of honor after you retire. The owner tells you in person, in the empty stadium, pointing at the spot.

choices.label: Call {parent} first
choices.result: {parent}, called before anyone else. He doesn't say anything for a long time, and then he asks you to describe the spot exactly.

choices.label: Ask them to wait
choices.result: Wait until you've actually retired, you ask. They agree, and it gives you something to look forward to on hard days.

choices.label: Ask to share it with the unit
choices.result: The long snapper and {holder}, you ask, should go up with you. The club agrees to think about it, and {holder} cries when you tell them.

scenarios.title: What's Next
scenarios.text: Your agent, {love_interest} and your accountant all ask you the same question in the same week of March, in almost exactly the same words: what's next?

choices.label: Make a real plan
choices.result: A real plan, on paper: three options, three timelines, one budget. It's the first time the future looks like something you can hold.

choices.label: Ask your family what they want
choices.result: Your family, asked directly what they want. Their answers change your whole list, and you're glad you asked before deciding anything.

choices.label: Answer after the season
choices.result: After the season, you tell everyone, and you mean it. You kick with a quiet mind, and the question waits patiently.

choices.label: Pull out the plan you already made
choices.result: You pull out the plan you started years ago. Most of it still fits, and the rest is easy to fix.
choices.lock_text: having prepared for life after football

scenarios.title: Betting to Cover It
scenarios.text: Your savings are thinner than anyone knows: an investment gone wrong, a house you can't sell, a payment due in March. An old acquaintance from home calls with an answer: one good week of bets, through him, and the hole closes.

choices.label: Hang up and call your advisor
choices.result: You hang up and call your advisor the same hour. The plan is slow and humbling, the house goes on the market at a loss, and you sleep for the first time in weeks.

choices.label: Tell {parent} how bad it is
choices.result: {parent} drives four hours that night and sits at your kitchen table with a calculator and a pot of coffee. By morning there's a plan, and you're not alone with it.

choices.label: Sell the thing you love
choices.result: The car you bought with your first big check goes to a dealer for less than it's worth. It stings every time you pass one like it, and the March payment is covered.

choices.label: Give him the money and the games
choices.result: The money and the names of three games go to him, none of them yours. For a month it works. Then the league's investigators find the account, and the commissioner's letter says a full season.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: One More
scenarios.text: At thirty-six, the next contract is one year at a time, and everyone in the building knows it, including the twenty-two-year-old kicker on the practice squad.

choices.label: Earn the next year every day
choices.result: Every practice treated as the interview it is. The coaches notice the veteran who never takes a rep off, and so does the rookie.

choices.label: Talk numbers honestly
choices.result: Your agent and you, talking numbers honestly: one year, fair money, and an out if your body says so. It's a calm conversation.

choices.label: Talk it over at home
choices.result: One more, you both say at the kitchen table, and you both mean it completely. {love_interest} squeezes your hand and doesn't let go.

scenarios.title: The Mentee Takes Your Job
scenarios.text: The kicker you taught is better than you now, everyone can see it, and {coach} wants to tell you before the depth chart comes out on Monday.

choices.label: Congratulate your old student
choices.result: You congratulate your old student before {coach} can finish. The kid is embarrassed and proud, and so are you, and you buy lunch.

choices.label: Fight for it
choices.result: Every day of camp, you fight for it. You lose, barely, and your old student says the competition made the difference for both of you.

choices.label: Ask about your role
choices.result: What's your role now? {coach}'s answer is honest: insurance, and the room's best teacher. It hurts, it's true, and you accept it.

scenarios.title: The One-Year Deal
scenarios.text: The offer is one year at the veteran minimum, delivered in a phone call that says, politely, take it or leave it. Your agent says nobody else has called.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.result: Signed. A year is a year, and you still love the work, and the first practice of the new season feels like a gift.

choices.label: Test the market
choices.result: The open market, tested for two weeks. Two clubs call, and one makes the same offer with more respect, and you sign with them.

choices.label: Ask home first
choices.result: {love_interest} asks you just one question: 'Do you still want it?' You do, and you sign the next morning without a second thought.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Talk
scenarios.text: It's late, the house is quiet, the kids are asleep, and {love_interest} finally asks the question you've both been walking around for a year: how many more seasons?

choices.label: Say one more
choices.result: You say one more season, and you mean it out loud for the first time. {love_interest} takes your hand, and suddenly every practice this year feels like a last one.

choices.label: Say you're not done
choices.result: It's not time yet, and you both know it. You agree to talk again after the season, and you sleep better than you have in weeks.

choices.label: Ask what they want
choices.result: You turn it around and ask what the next ten years should look like. It's the longest conversation you've had in months, and nobody mentions kicking until the very end.

choices.label: Bring out the old plan
choices.result: You find the plan you wrote in college for life after football. It's out of date and still mostly right, and the two of you rewrite it at the kitchen table until two in the morning.
choices.lock_text: having planned for life after football in college

scenarios.title: The Farewell Season
scenarios.text: Planning to retire after this season, you have to decide whether to tell the world now, or let it end quietly. Your agent has a press release drafted, just in case.

choices.label: Tell the world
choices.result: The announcement, made at the first press conference of the season. Every stadium has a sign for you, and every week becomes a long goodbye.

choices.label: Let it end quietly
choices.result: Quietly, and on your own terms. Only the people closest to you know, and that's exactly how you want your last season to feel.

choices.label: Tell the team only
choices.result: The team, told in a closed meeting. The specialists make it their mission to send you out right, and {holder} doesn't make it through the meeting dry-eyed.

scenarios.title: The Comeback Workout
scenarios.text: Released last spring, signed this summer at thirty-five by a club that needed a kicker fast. Everyone in camp, including some of the coaches, thinks you're finished.

choices.label: Show them on day one
choices.result: On the first day of camp, and every day after, you show them. By August, nobody calls you finished, and the youngest kicker asks for your routine.

choices.label: Help the young players
choices.result: From the first day, the young players get your help: film, rides, nerves. You're the veteran they didn't know they needed, and they say so.

choices.label: Let the numbers argue
choices.result: Every kick charted, and the numbers left on {coach}'s desk every Friday. They're good numbers, and they do the arguing for you.

scenarios.title: The Last Contract
scenarios.text: This contract is probably the last one. Your agent says so out loud, gently, while you're signing it in the general manager's office, and nobody says anything for a moment.

choices.label: Make it count
choices.result: Every single day of it counts: every practice, every rep, every quiet goodbye you aren't quite ready to say out loud yet.

choices.label: Plan the end
choices.result: You plan the end with your agent and your family, calmly, at the kitchen table. It's a little sad, and you sleep well that night.

choices.label: Celebrate it
choices.result: You celebrate it with dinner at the place you went after your first contract. The same waiter is there, older, and remembers you.

scenarios.title: Your Kid Wants to Kick
scenarios.text: Your kid, twelve now, wants to kick in middle school and asks you to teach them. They've been watching you in the backyard for years, and they already have your stance.

choices.label: Teach them in the backyard
choices.result: The backyard, every evening at six. They're better than you were at that age, and you don't tell them, yet.

choices.label: Keep it fun
choices.result: One tip a day and a lot of laughing. They fall in love with it the way you did, without pressure.

choices.label: Find them a good coach
choices.result: A good coach, found and hired, so you can just be the parent in the stands. It's harder than coaching, and better.

scenarios.title: Cleaning Out the Locker
scenarios.text: The box from your old locker is still in the trunk of your car, three weeks after the release. Nobody walked by while you packed it.

choices.label: Call someone from the old club
choices.result: {holder}, called from the parking lot of your new club. 'I should have come by,' they say. It helps more than you expected.

choices.label: Unpack it at the new place
choices.result: The box, unpacked at the new facility on the first day, into a new locker with the same routine. It feels like a fresh start.

choices.label: Leave it in the trunk
choices.result: The box stays in the trunk for a few more weeks. Some things take time, and you let them, and nobody asks.

scenarios.title: The Veteran Hearing
scenarios.text: Another hearing, years after the first one, and the union lawyer is younger than your snapper. The league's letter says it plainly: a veteran with your experience should have known better.

choices.label: Accept it without appeal
choices.result: Four games, no appeal. You practice with the scout team every day of it, early, and the young players notice how a veteran takes his punishment.

choices.label: Fight it
choices.result: You appeal and say the league is making an example of an old player. The appeal fails, the suspension doubles to eight games, and the story follows you to every road city.

choices.label: Accept it, and talk to the rookies
choices.result: Four games, accepted, and you ask the club to let you speak to the rookies about what it cost. The room is very quiet, and two of them thank you privately.
